# CHANGELOG · v1.1.0

Corrections applied to Volumes II, III, and IV. Every edit is listed with its count and its mechanism. Nothing was repaired silently. Source resolved from `1000sapients/Trisduction` at commit `5c0abfc`.

## 1 · One factual error

**Volume III, Chapter 76.** *Dawud AS Reubeni* → *David Reubeni*, 1 site. The figure is the sixteenth-century claimant, not the prophet Dawud AS. A name-normalisation pass had marked him as a prophet, which the volume's own front matter explicitly forbids: familiar English forms denoting a different person keep that person's name. Reubeni and the Himyarite king Yusuf As'ar Yath'ar are now both on that exception list. The error was present in the master and in the rendered PDF.

## 2 · One reported figure corrected

**Volume IV, corpus weight.** The stated ratio 48 / 8 / 42 was taken with an instrument recognising only citations that carry a book name. Books VIII and IX establish Mark once and then cite it bare, so the Gospel share was undercounted by roughly half and the Qur'ānic share inflated to match. Recounted under a stated instrument family: 49–56% Hebrew Bible, 7–13% Gospel, 31–43% Qur'ān, the spread being instrument sensitivity and printed as such. Volume III's ratio is stable across all three instruments and was correct as stated. Volume II is 100% Hebrew Bible under every instrument.

The correction is printed in the volume's own disclosure rather than made quietly, because the failure is the one this set already records against itself elsewhere: an instrument with no pattern for a category scores that category as absent, and the absence looks on the page exactly like a finding.

## 3 · Naming and honorific discipline

Each volume stated a naming rule its body did not keep. All three now state what they do and do what they state.

**Volume II** promised prophetic honorifics in its Reading Conventions and in Appendix L, then applied none across 166 chapters. Both clauses rewritten to state the actual and now-reasoned practice: the corpus is read in its own names and the honorific convention is deliberately suspended, as a consequence of the single-corpus constraint rather than an exception to it. Volume II now carries zero honorific marks and zero divine-name glyphs, which is what its own scope law requires.

**Volume III** promised one form of each name and ran two forms for four figures. Normalised to the declared list: Moses AS → Musa AS (3), Abraham AS → Ibrahim AS (4), Solomon AS → Sulayman AS (16), Joseph AS → Yusuf AS (5), the Joseph cycle → the Yusuf AS cycle (1), Noah's ark → the ark of Nuh AS (1), Aaron AS → Harun AS (1), Jacob AS → Yaʿqub AS (1), Elisha → Elisha AS (1). Two quotations carried an unmarked name against the volume's own rule that the honorific travels through quotation, at Mark 1:1 and at Josephus *Antiquities* 20.200; both now read ʿĪsā AS. The name-form clause was extended to cover Enoch AS, whose identification with Idris AS is traditional and not textual and is now typed as such, Elisha AS at Q 6:86 and 38:48, the figures the Qur'ān does not name as prophets and which therefore stand unmarked, and the adjectival forms, which are not names and are never marked.

**Volume IV** carried four naming systems at once and no stated rule. Diacritic doublets collapsed onto the declared plain forms, 16 sites across twelve names. English forms brought onto the list: Moses AS → Musa AS (10), Solomon AS → Sulayman AS (8), Joseph AS → Yusuf AS (2), Ishmael AS → Ismāʿīl AS (1). Prophets left entirely unmarked, now marked: David → Dawud AS (12 person sites, 3 of them possessive and rephrased), Elijah → Ilyas AS (22), Aaron → Harun AS (2), Jesus → ʿĪsā AS (3), Mary and bare Maryam → Maryam AS (2). Joshua unmarked at 7 sites to match Volume III and to keep the man from being marked wherever the book bearing his name is cited. Volume IV now carries the same naming clause as Volume III, together with Volume III's statement that the honorific is a reverence convention and not an argument, which Volume IV had lacked.

**Mechanism note.** The substring-replacement failure that produced the Reubeni error in the first place recurred during this pass and was caught by the same check: *Davidic* → *Dawud ASic* (10 sites) and *Aaronide* → *Harun ASide* (6 sites), both repaired and both now fenced by the adjectival clause in the front matter. Persons correctly left unmarked and verified as such: Mary Magdalene, Mary of Bethany, Moses of Crete, David Alroy, Abraham Abulafia, Solomon ibn Adret, Solomon Molcho, Isaac Luria, Rabbi Ishmael, Simon bar Jonah, Muhammad al-Mahdi, Yusuf As'ar Yath'ar, and the Jacob of the Matthean genealogy.

## 4 · Title collision resolved

Volume III's master opened with `# THE CONCEDED THRONE` while its rendered PDF titled it *History of the Messianic Position*, so master and render disagreed on which string was the title and the master's H1 collided head-on with Volume II. The master now leads with the messianic-position title, matching the PDF and the PDF metadata, and identifies itself as Volume III and a companion to *The Conceded Throne* rather than borrowing its name.

## 5 · The four volumes linked in the artifacts

A companion block was added to the front matter of all three, above the contents, stating the set, the reason there are four rather than one, the corpus admitted by each, the measured weights, Volume I's deposited DOIs, and the shared finding. In Volume II the block carries a fence: nothing in it is load-bearing, no chapter cites it, and the single-corpus constraint is unaffected. The block's one divine-name reference was rephrased so that inserting it into Volume II would not contradict the honorific suspension declared three pages earlier, and its cross-volume chapter pointer was made explicit so it does not read as a dangling internal reference.

## 6 · Disclosure

Volume II already carried a full author disclosure covering affiliation, funding, working method, audit history, and standing. Volumes III and IV carried none, which across a linked set reads as selective disclosure. Both now carry one on the same pattern, each with its own audit history and each carrying the corrections above on its own face.

**On Module VIII.** The publication discipline fires an Author's Provenance and Method Disclosure on public-facing paper deliverables, at LINE weight for the Journal edition, injecting the Trisduction master reference into the References section. That module was not fired here, deliberately. Its generic half asserts a specific verification architecture, its root axioms, and its named procedures, and its paper-specific half asks where the lock held with numbers. None of these three volumes was built through that pipeline; they were built philologically, with an AI as concordance and adversarial-audit instrument, which is what the disclosures now say. Injecting a method disclosure for a method not used would be a fabricated provenance and is the more serious defect of the two. The honest fix was to propagate Volume II's own disclosure. If the master reference is nonetheless wanted in these three, it is one line each and is the author's call, not the scribe's.

## 7 · Verified clean, unchanged

Structure holds in all three after the edits: contents match body one to one, 166 / 97 / 104 chapters, no missing or duplicate numbers, no dangling chapter, appendix, or excursus references, no glued-token damage. All Qur'ānic citations fall inside valid sura and verse ranges. Falsification loops close in all three. Textual overlap between the three volumes is under 0.2 percent by shingle, confirming they are three independent compositions and not three renderings of one, so three separate deposits are correct and no supersession is owed.

## 8 · Not done, and why

The rendered PDFs in the parent folder were built from the pre-correction masters and are now stale in body, front matter, and end matter. They must be re-rendered from this folder before any deposit.

Volume I was not modified. Its PDF is immutable at version DOI `10.5281/zenodo.22243674`, and adding the companion block to its git master would put git and Zenodo out of step for no gain. The set linkage for Volume I belongs in that record's `related_identifiers` metadata, which is editable without a new version.

The session bundle `The Conceded Throne · complete session bundle.zip` is a working artifact. It belongs in git and on neither deposit surface.
# FINAL v1.1.0 · The Four-Volume Set

Corrected masters, audit-clean, ready for re-render and deposit. These supersede the loose files in the parent folder for Volumes II, III, and IV. Volume I is already deposited and is not modified here.

## Why there are four

A reader inside one tradition will not accept another tradition's scripture as evidence, and is right not to. Building one volume that cites all three canons and asking every reader to grant the other two is a request, not a method. So the office is read four times. Volume I is a geopolitical and archaeological audit that adjudicates no scripture. Above it the same position is read three times, once inside each corpus, by the same instrument, each reading answerable to its own canon alone. The structural and linguistic finding is the same in all three and is reached three separate times on three disjoint bodies of evidence. The geometry stands on its own ground. The scriptures are witnesses on their own.

## Naming conventions across the set

Volumes III and IV carry one form of each prophetic name, drawn from a stated list, with the honorific travelling through quotation. The honorific is a reverence convention and not an argument: it asserts no corpus's reading of any figure and decides nothing in either direction. Figures the Qur'ān does not name as prophets keep their corpus form and carry no mark, which is why Joshua, Samuel, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, and Ezra stand unmarked. Adjectival forms are never marked.

Volume II carries no honorifics at all and states why: a study admitting the Hebrew Bible alone as evidence should not carry, in its running text, a naming convention drawn from a corpus it has excluded. The suspension is a consequence of the single-corpus constraint rather than an exception to it, and nothing interpretive follows from it in either direction.

## One item left open

The set has no series title. Each volume names the other three and states the relation, which is sufficient for a reader and for a Zenodo `related_identifiers` block. A series title is an identity act and is the author's to make, not the scribe's. If one is wanted it should be settled before the first of the three is minted, because a series statement added after minting will not appear in the earlier records.
# HISTORY OF THE MESSIANIC POSITION IN THE JEWISH, CHRISTIAN, AND QUR'ANIC RECORDS

### The Figure Grows. The Deficit Does Not Move.

#### Volume III of four · Companion to *The Conceded Throne*

---

## A NOTE ON WHAT THIS BOOK IS

This is not a biography.

A biography has a subject. It follows one life from a beginning to an end, and its coherence comes from the fact that a single person was there the whole time to be followed. Almost every book written about the Messiah has been organised that way, whether it presents him as a man who came, a man who is coming, or a man who is coming back. The organising assumption is the same in all three cases: there is a figure, and the sources are testimony about him.

This book is organised the other way around. Its subject is a **position**, not a person. The position is described in the Hebrew scriptures with unusual precision, offered repeatedly, and, by the testimony of those same scriptures, never entered. Everything written afterwards, across a millennium of Jewish literature, four centuries of Christian formation, and fourteen centuries of claimants in three religions, is read here as the record of what a community does with an unoccupied position it cannot abandon.

The difference is not a matter of tone. It changes what counts as evidence. In a biography, a second-century rabbinic tradition naming the Messiah's pre-existent soul is evidence about the Messiah. In a history of a position, the same tradition is evidence about the second century: about what the position had come to require by then, and about the pressure that made the requirement necessary. The first reading treats the source as a window. The second treats it as a measurement. This book takes every source as a measurement, and the resulting curve is the argument.

The curve has a shape, and the shape is the finding. Across the whole record, in every corpus, the figure who is to fill the position grows. He begins as a man anointed with oil by a prophet, an ordinary Iron Age office holder whose title says only that oil was poured on him. He becomes a dynastic guarantee, then a surviving remnant, then a branch from a cut stump, then a pre-existent name written before the world, then a soul stored in a heavenly treasury, then a figure to whom dominion is given in a night vision, then a being through whom the world was made. At each stage the agent offered against the problem is larger than at the last.

And the problem does not move.

That is the whole book in one sentence, and it is worth stating at the outset so the reader can watch for it and can watch for its failure. **The escalation of the figure is an enlargement of the agent offered against a deficit that is not located in the agent.** The Hebrew scriptures locate the deficit precisely, name it repeatedly, and say what it is: the rest was completed and handed over, and what failed was entry. Nothing in the record says the rest was insufficient. Everything in the record says it was not entered. An enlarged deliverer answers a problem the texts do not report having.

Whether that finding survives is the reader's judgement to make, and the book is built so it can be made. Three things are stated at the front for that purpose. First, the thesis is stated once, in Book I, and then demonstrated rather than repeated. Second, every claim carries its evidentiary weight visibly, so a reader can see which load a given rung is bearing and refuse it if the rung will not hold. Third, three specific findings would break the argument, and they are printed in Book I with the evidence that would settle each. A book that cannot be broken has not said anything.

One more thing belongs here, because it governs the ending. This book does not name a man at the end. It does not name one because the record does not, and because the position of an instrument that cannot name one is to say so rather than to supply a name and call the supply a conclusion. The argument runs to a boundary, locates it exactly, describes what stands on this side of it, and stops. Readers who require a verdict on an identity will find the boundary instead. The boundary is the honest result and the book says why at length in its final movement.

---

## READING CONVENTIONS

**Honorifics.** The formulae following the divine and prophetic names are components of the names in this book and are not decorations that may be dropped for brevity. Allah ﷻ carries the glorification. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ carries the blessing. Every other prophet carries AS. They travel unaltered through every translation, quotation, table, and summary in every book below, including passages drawn from Hebrew, Aramaic, Greek, and Latin sources, and including material quoted from writers hostile to the figure named.

**The forms of the prophetic names.** One form of each name is used throughout, whichever corpus is being read, so that a reader following a figure across three canons is following one name. The forms are: Adam AS, Nuh AS, Ibrahim AS, Ismāʿīl AS, Ishaq AS, Yaʿqub AS, Yusuf AS, Musa AS, Harun AS, Dawud AS, Sulayman AS, Ilyas AS, Yunus AS, Zakariyya AS, Yahya AS, and ʿĪsā AS. Maryam AS carries the same mark. Where a name in this list stands in a quotation from a Hebrew, Greek, or Latin text, the form given here is used and the honorific travels with it; the underlying text is unaffected and is given in transliteration where the wording matters. Where a familiar English form denotes a different person entirely, that person keeps his own name: Moses of Crete, David Alroy, David Reubeni, Abraham Abulafia, Solomon ibn Adret, Solomon Molcho, and the Himyarite king Yusuf As'ar Yath'ar are not prophets and carry no mark. Book titles keep their conventional forms: 1 Enoch, the Psalms of Solomon, the Wisdom of Solomon, the Testament of Solomon. Two prophets are carried in the form their corpus uses, because the reading requires it and a reader would otherwise lose the passage: Enoch AS, whom the tradition identifies with Idris AS at traditional and not textual grade, and Elisha AS, al-Yasaʿ at Q 6:86 and 38:48. Figures the Qur'an does not name as prophets keep their corpus form and carry no mark, which is why Joshua, Samuel, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, and Ezra stand unmarked throughout; in the case of Joshua the book bearing the name would otherwise be marked along with the man. Adjectival forms derived from a name are not names and are never marked: Davidic, Aaronide, Solomonic, Mosaic.

**The corpora and their names.** The Hebrew scriptures are cited by their Hebrew-canonical book names and chapter and verse. Where a Greek or Latin tradition numbers a verse differently, the Hebrew numbering governs and the variant is noted at first occurrence. The Gospels and the apostolic writings are cited by their conventional names. The Qur'an is cited as Q by sura and verse. Second Temple, rabbinic, patristic, and medieval works are cited by title and locus.

**Transliteration.** Hebrew and Arabic are given in a plain transliteration without diacritical apparatus except where a consonant distinction carries the argument, in which case the distinction is marked and explained at the point of use. Roots are given in the form used by their own grammatical tradition: Hebrew and Arabic triliterals by their three consonants, Greek by lemma.

**Evidence marking.** Every substantive claim in this book carries one of six labels, and the labels are cumulative rather than rhetorical.

*Documented* means a primary text says it, in the language of the text, and the citation is exact.

*Attested* means a source of the relevant period reports it, and the report is what is being cited rather than the fact behind the report.

*Reconstructed* means the claim is an inference from what several sources jointly require, stated as inference.

*Disputed* means competent readers of the same evidence disagree, and the disagreement is named rather than resolved by preference.

*Circumstantial* means the claim is supported by context and pattern rather than by direct statement.

*Speculative* means the claim is offered as a possibility with its supporting considerations and nothing stronger.

**The strength rule that governs those labels.** A conclusion is never stronger than the weakest source it actually leans on. If a reading requires a canonical verse and a sixth-century commentary jointly, and the commentary is doing real work, the reading is as strong as the commentary and no stronger. This rule is applied throughout without exception, and it retires a great many claims that are usually presented as settled. Where it retires something, the retirement is visible, because a book that quietly drops what it cannot support is less useful than one that shows the drop.

**Source priority.** Each canon is read first from inside itself. The Hebrew scriptures are read against the Hebrew scriptures before any later Jewish or Christian reading of them is admitted. The Gospels are read against the Gospels. The Qur'an is read against the Qur'an. This is not a devotional preference but an evidentiary one: the interpretive corpus of every tradition postdates its scripture by centuries, was formed under political conditions that are documented, and reached us through schools that were in open conflict with one another and that discredited one another's transmissions. No such corpus can be treated as a neutral pipe. Later interpretation enters this book as testimony about the period that produced it, which is exactly the office in which it is most valuable and where its evidentiary value is highest rather than lowest.

**Cross-corpus reading.** When two canons are read against each other, neither is subordinated to the other. Where they converge, the convergence is reported as convergence between two independent witnesses. Where they diverge, the divergence is reported and neither is corrected by the other. Silence in one canon about something another canon states is silence, and is never read as denial.

## THE FOUR VOLUMES, AND WHY THERE ARE FOUR

This volume is one of four. They share a conclusion and they do not share a corpus, and the second fact is the reason the first is worth anything.

A reader inside one tradition will not accept another tradition's scripture as evidence, and is right not to. A Jewish reader owes nothing to a Gospel citation and nothing to a Qurʾānic one. A Christian reader reading the Hebrew corpus is entitled to see it read on its own terms before it is read as prologue to anything. A Muslim reader is entitled to the Qurʾānic account read from inside the Qurʾān rather than as a late gloss on someone else's book. Building one volume that cites all three canons and asking every reader to grant the other two is not a method. It is a request.

So the office is read four times instead of once. The ground floor is a geopolitical and archaeological audit that touches no theology and adjudicates no scripture. Above it the same position is read three times, once inside each corpus, by the same instrument, with each reading answerable to its own canon alone. Each reading is answerable to its own corpus alone, so a reader who grants only one of the three canons can check that volume on its own terms and owes nothing to the other two. The convergence is one author's finding reproduced on three disjoint bodies of evidence under that constraint, and it is offered as exactly that, a reproduction under a stated constraint, never as three independent witnesses. The scriptures are the witnesses, each on its own ground.

**The structural and linguistic finding is the same in all three, and it is reached three separate times on three disjoint bodies of evidence.** The position is stated with precision, offered repeatedly, and never entered. The failure is located at the receiver and never at the agent. The figure offered against that failure grows without limit while the failure stands where it stood. And the grammar by which the figure receives what he holds never changes: the verb is passive, or the divine name is the subject.

The geometry stands on its own ground. The scriptures are witnesses on their own. Neither is asked to underwrite the other, and a reader may take one volume and leave the other three without losing the argument.

**Measured corpus weight**, counted under a stated instrument family and printed as a range because the figure is instrument-sensitive: a citation is counted when it carries a book name, full or standardly abbreviated, and a bare chapter-and-verse reference is resolved to the nearest named book above it or to the book that dominates its chapter. A named-book count alone undercounts a corpus cited bare after its book has been established, which is a defect this set caught in its own earlier figures and records here rather than repairing silently. A count recognising only unabbreviated book names returns 49, 9, and 43 for Volume IV, and that sensitivity is printed rather than hidden:

|---|---|---|---|

Volume I is the archaeological and geopolitical floor and carries no scriptural adjudication, so it takes no row.

**Volume I is deposited** at Zenodo under version DOI `10.5281/zenodo.22243674`, concept DOI `10.5281/zenodo.22243673`, CC BY 4.0. Volumes II, III, and IV form one set and each carries this block; their identifiers are recorded in the folder's README as they are minted.

**What the volumes do not do.** None of them names a man at the end. None predicts an arrival and none rests on non-arrival. Volume II states this at Chapter 164 of that volume, and Volumes III and IV state it in their own closing movements. A reader looking for a book that argues against a messiah has picked up the wrong set, and a reader looking for one that argues for one has too.
